newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canada monetary stimulus hits all-time high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canada monetary stimulus hits all-time high.

text.p: Canadian monetary conditions, as measured by a key Bank of Canada indicator, soared to their most stimulative levels on record on Wednesday.

But analysts said that the move in the bank's monetary conditions index (MCI) -- a mixture of short-term interest rates and currency strength -- would not necessarily prompt the central bank to tighten rates.

"There is absolutely no particular level (in the MCI) at which you can be certain the Bank of Canada will move either way and there never has been," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research with TD Securities Inc.
The MCI as calculated by Reuters reached an all-time low of - 6.29 on Wednesday. A negative MCI number indicates stimulative conditions, while a positive number shows they are restrictive.
The indicator is made up of the three-month commercial paper rate and the trade-weighted Canadian dollar.
It has set several record lows this year with the Bank of Canada keeping short-term interest rates at their lowest level in decades even as the currency weakened.
The currency is included in the calculation because its movements, like rate changes, affect Canada's export-oriented economy.

Many market watchers had expected the MCI to begin tightening in the past month after the Bank of Canada said it would like conditions tightened over the medium term. The central bank also predicted the Canadian dollar would gradually strengthen, a trend that would tighten monetary conditions.
Instead the currency weakened, with investors now awaiting an interest rate hike by the Bank of Canada before sending the currency higher.

Dan Kelly, director of financial markets research with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc, said the Bank of Canada would like to see the monetary conditions index tighter, but did not want to hike rates until it saw more signs of economic strength.

"We still have an over 9 percent unemployment rate, so I don't think the Bank of Canada is in any great hurry to try and choke this off," said Kelly. He noted that the weakness in the MCI was something the Bank of Canada tolerated rather than encouraged.

Analysts said other evidence suggesting the central bank would not hike rates to offset the move in the MCI included comments by Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Chuck Freedman last month that the central bank had no formal target range for the MCI and did not focus on it in a "mechanistic" fashion.
He said the MCI was one of a number of tools the bank used to determine actions affecting monetary policy.
Only a clear downward trend in the Canadian dollar -- which could not be stopped by direct intervention -- would prompt the central bank to hike short-term rates, analysts said.

"I don't think it (the bank) is ready to take short-term rates up yet on fundamental grounds," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "But if they are unable to prevent the currency from further weakness and there's further loosening of MCI, then I think the Bank's got little choice but to come through with an adjustment to the overnight rate."
